title: A contrast knob on the odds
allegory: Temperature is like a contrast knob on the model's odds: low temperature is high contrast, so the likeliest word outshines the rest; high temperature is low contrast, so every word fades towards the same grey; and the order of brightness never changes.
map: the temperature T that divides the logits
high contrast: the brightest lamp outshines all
T < 1: the distribution sharpens towards the argmax
low contrast: everything fades to grey
T > 1: the distribution flattens towards uniform
z/T is monotone, so the ranking and any top-k set are unchanged
credit: The temperature-slider view, from 'always the most predictable word' at T = 0 to wilder text as T rises, is borrowed from 3Blue1Brown, 'But what is a GPT?' (Deep Learning, chapter 5).

cap.1: Ask the same model the same thing twice and get a dull answer or a wild one. The difference is one knob, and it touches nothing inside the model.
cap.2: Temperature changes how you sample from the model's next-token distribution, not the model. Low: predictable and repetitive. High: varied, then incoherent.
cap.3: Temperature is a decoding hyperparameter: it rescales the logits before the softmax. Same forward pass, different sampling distribution.

cap.1: Picture the model's options as lamps, brighter for likelier words. Temperature is a contrast knob: it exaggerates or softens the differences, never the order.
cap.2: Divide every logit by T, then softmax. T < 1 stretches the gaps, so the favourite takes more of the probability. T > 1 squashes the gaps towards a flat distribution.
cap.3: softmax(z/T)ᵢ = pᵢ^(1/T) / Σⱼ pⱼ^(1/T): a power curve on the probabilities. Rank order is invariant because z ↦ z/T is strictly monotone for T > 0.

cap.1: Before the scores become odds, divide them all by T. That single division is the whole feature.
cap.2: apply_temperature is one line: logits / temperature. A small T makes the gaps between scores bigger; a big T makes them smaller.
cap.3: Gaps scale as Δz/T, and the odds between two tokens are exp(Δz/T). So T = 0.5 squares every odds ratio and T = 2 takes its square root.

cap.1: As T drops towards 0, the favourite's share climbs to 100%: always the top word. As T grows, the two options drift towards a coin flip.
cap.2: Two tokens with a logit gap Δz: the favourite's probability is sigmoid(Δz/T). T near 0 gives greedy decoding, large T gives uniform, T = 1 is the model's own distribution.
cap.3: p = σ(Δz/T), with limits argmax as T → 0⁺ and uniform as T → ∞. Code usually special-cases T = 0 as argmax, since dividing by zero is undefined.

chapters.name: It cannot reorder
chapters.verdict: They compound, not trade off: low T plus top-k can loop.

cap.1: No contrast setting can relight a lamp that was switched off. With top-k the tail is already gone, and low temperature hands nearly all of it to one word.
cap.2: T never reorders tokens, so it cannot change which survive top-k. Low T after truncation piles the mass on the argmax: that is how 'more focused' turns into loops.
cap.3: sample_next_token applies frequency penalty, then temperature, then top-k/top-p. T only rescales within the truncated support, so low T with small k is close to greedy.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Low T for reliable answers, higher for variety
T changes the draw, not the model
Fix and report T in every eval

cap.1: Temperature changes how you draw from the model, not what it believes. To understand a model, look at its odds, not one lucky or unlucky sample.
cap.2: When you evaluate or red-team a model, fix and report the temperature, because results shift with it. Interpretability work reads the logits directly instead.
cap.3: T only reweights an existing distribution; it reveals nothing new about the model. For evals, fix T and sample enough; for interpretability, work with logits or log-probs.

coda.title: Turn the contrast knob on GPT-2's top five guesses

caption.1: GPT-2's top five guesses after 'John and Mary went to the'. Drag T left and 'church' swallows everything; drag right and they even out. The order never changes.
caption.2: Real top-5 probabilities from ARENA's calibration check, renormalised. Halving T squares the odds ratio; raising T takes roots. Watch the greedy readout flip past 90%.
caption.3: Bars = softmax(log p / T) over the top-5 support, i.e. top_k=5 then temperature. Odds ratios scale as r^(1/T); the ranking is invariant; above about 0.9 top share you are effectively greedy.

where_else: Scaled attention: dividing QKᵀ by √d_k acts as a fixed temperature that keeps the softmax from saturating
Knowledge distillation, where a higher temperature exposes more of a teacher's preferences
Softmax policies in RL, where a temperature trades exploring against exploiting
The Boltzmann distribution in physics, where the name comes from

hamming.what: A single number that divides the logits before the softmax, sharpening (T < 1) or flattening (T > 1) the next-token distribution.
hamming.when: Every time you sample from a model: low for reliable, repeatable answers, higher for variety.
hamming.why: It trades predictability against diversity without changing the model or the ranking of its guesses.

object.title: The temperature terrace
object.subtitle: The same five guesses at five temperatures: a spike when cold, a plateau when hot, the same order in every row.

cap.1: Each row is the same five guesses at a different temperature. Cold rows are one tall spike; hot rows are nearly flat.
cap.2: Rows: T from 0.25 to 4. Columns: GPT-2's top five next words. Height: probability.
cap.3: softmax(log p / T) per row; the argmax column is the same in every row.

cap.1: From the front: the order of the bars never changes, only how steeply they fall.
cap.2: Temperature is monotone, so the ranking is identical in every row.
cap.3: z ↦ z/T preserves the argsort; only the entropy moves, from near 0 when cold towards log 5 when hot.

cap.1: Cut to the top two. No temperature can bring the other three back.
cap.2: top_k=2 zeroes three columns in every row; T only reshares the two survivors.
cap.3: Truncation fixes the support and T reweights within it, so the two knobs compound.

cap.1: Cold plus a tight cut: 'church' takes almost everything. That is how loops begin.
cap.2: Low T after truncation is nearly greedy: the renormalised top share passes 0.9.
cap.3: At T = 0.25 and k = 2 the argmax holds r⁴/(1 + r⁴) of the mass with r = 0.0648/0.0367, about 0.91.

cap.1: Pick one knob: to focus, lower k and keep T at 1, or keep T low and add a frequency penalty to break loops.
cap.2: Hold T = 1 and lower k, or use top-p. A frequency penalty reorders logits, which T and k never do.
cap.3: Only the frequency penalty, applied before T, changes rank order, so it alone can break a loop that low T and small k create.

predict.q: You lower T from 1 to 0.5. Can a token outside the top 5 move into the top 5?

options.t: No: dividing by T never changes the order
Yes: low T reshuffles the ranking

predict.why: z/T is monotone for T > 0, so the ranking and any top-k set stay identical.

predict.q: At T = 0.5, what happens to the odds ratio between two tokens?
predict.why: Odds are exp(Δz/T). Halving T doubles the exponent, which squares the ratio.

predict.q: Generations loop at low T with top-k. Which knob can actually break the loop?

options.t: A frequency penalty, which reorders the logits

predict.why: A bigger k adds tokens whose share rounds to nothing at low T. Only the frequency penalty changes the order.

object.where: Anywhere a softmax turns scores into choices: sampling, scaled attention, distillation, Boltzmann exploration.
